templates.name: Period between independent clauses (second often opens with an introductory phrase)
Conjunctive adverb: semicolon or period on the correct side, comma on the other
Colon after a complete clause before an explanation or specified item
No punctuation with a restrictive clause or restrictive appositive
Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
Items in a series (commas; semicolons when items contain commas)
Comma before a trailing nonrestrictive modifier
Comma or parenthesis pair around a supplementary element
No punctuation between subject and verb
No punctuation between a verb or preposition and its object
Question versus statement (word order and end mark)

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a long noun-phrase appositive
items.passage: In 2002, researchers exploring California’s Monterey Canyon with a remotely operated vehicle discovered a gray whale skeleton covered in what looked like small red ______ with neither a mouth nor a gut, these animals penetrate the bones with rootlike tissues that house symbiotic bacteria.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 2002, researchers ... discovered a gray whale skeleton covered in what looked like small red plumes” is a complete sentence. “Worms with neither a mouth nor a gut” describes “these animals,” the subject of the next sentence (“these animals penetrate the bones ...”), so a period is needed after “plumes.”

A.why_wrong: The comma lets “worms with neither a mouth nor a gut” read as a description of “plumes,” but “these animals penetrate the bones” is a second independent clause, so the two clauses are joined by a comma alone.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together and “plumes worms” garbles the first one.

C.why_wrong: “that were worms with neither a mouth nor a gut” attaches to “plumes,” but “these animals penetrate the bones ...” still follows with only a comma, so the result is a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: science (deep-sea biology, the bone-eating worm Osedax, found on a whale fall in 2002). Band 7: an 8-word noun-phrase opener (0fa289a7, 940ff6f7 shape) that reads as an appositive to “plumes” in A and C; the splice shows only at “these animals,” 9 words past the blank; one 44-word run. Menu of the models (splice, glued, added “that were”); no semicolon option. Researchers unnamed.
band7_moves: opener is an 8-word noun phrase that could rename clause 1's last noun
clause 2's subject arrives 9 words past the blank, outside a 6-word window
added-word option ('that were') keeps a splice

band7.why: S1_period on 0fa289a7: the 8-word noun-phrase opener “Worms with neither a mouth nor a gut” reads as an appositive to “plumes” in A and C, and the splice shows only at “these animals,” 9 words past the blank; 44-word run; splice, glued and added “that were” menu as in 0fa289a7.

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a because-clause
items.passage: In 1999, construction workers quarrying gravel in Veracruz, Mexico, unearthed a serpentine slab incised with 62 ______ several of these symbols recur in consistent sequences, much as words do, many specialists regard the slab, now called the Cascajal Block, as the earliest known example of writing in the Americas.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 1999, construction workers ... unearthed a serpentine slab incised with 62 signs” is a complete sentence. The next sentence is “Because several of these symbols recur ..., many specialists regard the slab ... as the earliest known example of writing in the Americas”: the because-clause introduces its main clause, “many specialists regard,” so a period goes after “signs.”

A.why_wrong: The comma makes the because-clause seem to explain the first sentence, but “many specialists regard the slab ...” is then a second independent clause joined by a comma alone.

C.why_wrong: Without punctuation the because-clause attaches to the first clause, and “many specialists regard the slab ...” follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “that” would start a relative clause about the signs, but the words after it (“many specialists regard the slab ...”) form a complete clause with nothing missing, so the sentence is ungrammatical.

items.notes: Subject: history (Olmec-era inscribed slab from Veracruz, reported in 2006). Band 7: clause 2 opens with a subordinator (615f001e), so A and C read as a natural because-clause on clause 1 until “many specialists” arrives 13 words past the blank; the because-clause carries its own “much as” interrupter. No semicolon or “and” option (each would make a correct sentence). No researcher named.
band7_moves: clause 2 opens with a subordinate clause, so the comma reads as legal
clause 2's subject arrives 13 words past the blank

band7.why: 615f001e move: clause 2 opens with “Because,” so “, because” and “ because” read as a legal subordinate clause on clause 1 until “many specialists regard” arrives 13 words past the blank; 49-word run; added-word “that,” option.

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second sentence's subject is a gerund phrase
items.passage: In 1978, faced with a shortage of incubators, doctors at a maternity hospital in Bogotá, Colombia, began asking mothers of premature infants to carry their babies against their bare ______ newborns skin-to-skin in this way stabilized their temperature and encouraged breastfeeding, and the method, called kangaroo mother care, has since spread worldwide.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “to carry their babies against their bare chests.” In the second sentence, the gerund phrase “Holding newborns skin-to-skin in this way” is the subject of “stabilized,” so it must begin a new sentence after a period.

A.why_wrong: The comma makes “holding newborns skin-to-skin” look like a phrase describing the mothers, which leaves “stabilized their temperature” without a subject; read as a subject, the phrase starts a second clause joined by a comma alone.

B.why_wrong: “while holding newborns skin-to-skin in this way” attaches to the first clause, so the verb “stabilized” is left with no subject.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “chests holding newborns ...” runs the two sentences together, and “stabilized” has no subject.

items.notes: Subject: science (medicine: kangaroo mother care, begun in Bogotá in 1978). Band 6: gerund-subject opener (73a6603c) with a different menu (while-phrase and glued options instead of “; by adding”); the comma version reads as a participle on the mothers until “stabilized” 6 words past the blank. No semicolon option. Doctors unnamed.

fixes: explanation and why_wrong for A, B and D quoted “kept” / “kept them warm”, which the passage does not contain; now “stabilized” / “stabilized their temperature”

band7.why: Target 6. Gerund-subject opener (73a6603c, band 6); the comma version reads as a participle on the mothers until “stabilized” 7 words past the blank, but a gerund subject is the band-6 opener type, not the band-7 appositive that could rename clause 1’s last noun.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing clause 1 (contrast with the previous sentence), semicolon after it
items.passage: The trap-jaw ant Odontomachus bauri, native to Central and South American rainforests, captures prey by releasing its spring-loaded mandibles, which snap shut at velocities of up to 64 meters per second. Those mandibles serve more than a predatory ______ an ant that strikes them against the ground can catapult itself away from potential attackers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence presents the mandibles as a way to capture prey, and “Those mandibles serve more than a predatory function” runs against that, so “however” belongs at the end of this clause, set off by a comma. The semicolon then joins the clause to the next one, “an ant that strikes them against the ground can catapult itself away from potential attackers,” which gives the other use.

B.why_wrong: Placing “however” at the start of the second clause signals a contrast between “serve more than a predatory function” and “an ant ... can catapult itself away from potential attackers,” but the second clause is an example of the first, not a contrast with it.

C.why_wrong: With commas on both sides of “however,” the two independent clauses are joined by commas alone.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma before “however” and with only a comma after it, the two independent clauses are still joined by a comma alone.

items.notes: Subject: science (ant biomechanics; jaw speeds of 35 to 64 meters per second, escape jumps). Band 7: “however” closes clause 1, which corrects the impression left by sentence 1 (mandibles for capturing prey); B, the taught “; however,” placement, fails only on meaning, the cue sitting in the previous sentence. “however” is never offered in a position where it could read as “in whatever way” (D keeps a comma after it), and no “though” option (b2 lesson). No researcher named.
band7_moves: adverb closes clause 1, which answers the previous sentence
clause 2 elaborates clause 1, so no contrast reading of B survives

review.note: “; however,” option (B) judged not defensible, so kept as the band-7 logic trap: clause 2 (the escape jump) is the non-predatory function clause 1 announces, so “however” between them has nothing to contrast; same relation as c06af4d8 and b771d175, whose “; however,” distractors fail the same way. Unlike the b2 “, though” case, “however” here can never read as a subordinator (D keeps a comma after it).

band7.why: c06af4d8 and b771d175 shape: “however” closes clause 1, which corrects the predatory framing of sentence 1; B, the taught “; however,” placement, fails only on meaning with the cue in the previous sentence; C and D are splices. The 26-word run is short of the band-7 range, as in the official adverb items.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing clause 1, period after it
items.passage: Livonian, a Finnic language once spoken in fishing villages along Latvia’s coast, lost its last native speaker, Grizelda Kristiņa, in 2013. The language hasn’t ______ descendants of Livonian families in Latvia continue to study it, and linguists have compiled dictionaries and grammars to support its revitalization.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The language hasn’t disappeared, however” contrasts with the first sentence’s news that the last native speaker died, so “however” ends that clause, set off by a comma. A period then begins the next sentence, “Many descendants of Livonian families in Latvia continue to study it ...,” which supports the claim that the language survives.

A.why_wrong: “however” at the start of the second clause would signal a contrast between the language not disappearing and descendants studying it, but the second clause supports the first.

B.why_wrong: Commas alone on both sides of “however” join two independent clauses, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no comma before “however,” the adverb runs into the first clause, and the two independent clauses are joined by a comma alone.

items.notes: Subject: language (Livonian after its last native speaker died in 2013). Band 6: “however. Many” key (2bb7416a shape) with a different menu: one logic-wrong option plus two splices, no fused “however many” (which would read as “no matter how many” and could be grammatical). Details kept general (descendants studying it, dictionaries and grammars).

review.note: “; however,” option (A) judged not defensible: clause 2 (descendants study it, linguists compiled dictionaries to support its revitalization) supports “The language hasn’t disappeared,” so “however” between them has nothing to contrast; same relation as b771d175 (“Compiling isn’t exclusive...; however, any language can incorporate this tool”). No “ however many” option, which could read as “no matter how many.”

band7.why: Target 6. “however. Many” key (2bb7416a, band 6) with one logic-wrong “; however,” option and two splices; the period key is the band-6 adverb shape, not the band-7 clause-1 “, however;” key.

items.subtype: Colon before a specified item, then a period before the next sentence
items.passage: Goffin’s cockatoos feed on the seeds of the sea mango, which are protected by a tough, fibrous husk. To extract them, the birds employ a technique previously documented in the wild in only one other ______ up to three distinct tools from branches, a cockatoo applies them in a particular sequence to reach the seed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “To extract them, the birds employ a technique previously documented in the wild in only one other species” is a complete clause, so a colon can introduce the species it refers to, “the chimpanzee.” A period must then end that sentence, because “Fashioning up to three distinct tools from branches” introduces the subject of a new sentence, “a cockatoo applies them in a particular sequence ....”

A.why_wrong: The commas make “the chimpanzee” an appositive, but “a cockatoo applies them in a particular sequence ...” is then a second independent clause joined by a comma alone.

B.why_wrong: After the semicolon, “the chimpanzee, fashioning up to three distinct tools from branches, a cockatoo applies ...” has two subjects for one verb, so it isn't a complete clause.

D.why_wrong: The new sentence “The chimpanzee, fashioning up to three distinct tools from branches, a cockatoo applies them in a particular sequence ...” has two subjects (“The chimpanzee” and “a cockatoo”) for one verb, so it is ungrammatical.

items.notes: Subject: science (wild Goffin's cockatoo tool sets, reported in 2021; tool sets were previously documented in the wild only in chimpanzees). Band 7: the 3a2d77d7 move (colon then period in one option), each distractor right at one slot; the doubled subject that kills B and D shows only at “a cockatoo,” 9 words past the blank. No lone-dash option. Researchers unnamed.
band7_moves: colon and period in one option (3a2d77d7)
each distractor is right at one of the two slots
the doubled subject appears 9 words past the blank

fixes: explanation and why_wrong for A and D quoted “applies them in sequence”; now “in a particular sequence” as in the passage
D recipe relabelled from “doubled subject after a period” (not a report recipe) to “misplaced boundary” (the period puts “The chimpanzee” on the wrong side, as in 3a2d77d7)

band7.why: 3a2d77d7 move: colon and period in one option, each distractor right at one of the two slots; the fault in A, B and D shows only at “a cockatoo,” 9 words past the blank; 55-word passage.

items.subtype: Restrictive appositive (non-person): no punctuation between a noun and the name that identifies it
items.passage: Roughly 200 million mounds, each about 2.5 meters tall, are spaced at strikingly regular intervals across a vast region of northeastern Brazil. In 2018, researchers reported that the mounds, some nearly 4,000 years old, are not nests but piles of soil that the ______ removed while excavating networks of underground tunnels.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Syntermes dirus” identifies which termite produced the mounds; without it, “the termite” would not say which one is meant. Because the name is essential, it is not set off with commas. No punctuation can come between the subject “the termite Syntermes dirus” and its verb, “removed.”

A.why_wrong: The comma before the name opens an interruption that is never closed, and it separates an essential name from the noun it identifies.

C.why_wrong: The commas treat “Syntermes dirus” as extra information, but the name is needed to identify the termite.

D.why_wrong: The comma separates the subject “the termite Syntermes dirus” from its verb, “removed.”

items.notes: Subject: science (the Caatinga termite mounds of northeastern Brazil, reported in 2018). Band 7: the non-person restrictive appositive of 59a246dc (“the chemical compound aluminum oxide”), set inside a relative clause so a comma also falls between subject and verb in D. Local by nature (the band-7 file exempts S4_restrictive from the cue-distance check). Researchers unnamed.
band7_moves: commas around the name look polite
the appositive sits inside a relative clause, subject before its verb

band7.why: 59a246dc move: a non-person restrictive appositive, “the termite Syntermes dirus,” followed directly by its verb, so the commas in C look polite and D puts a comma between subject and verb; local by nature, which the band-7 file exempts from the cue-distance check.

items.subtype: Restrictive that-clause: no commas around it or between it and the verb
items.passage: Taíno caciques, or chiefs, presided over ceremonial gatherings seated on duhos, low seats carved from a single piece of hardwood or stone. The ______ frequently display a human or animal face at the front, while the seat’s elongated back curves upward behind it like a tail.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: duhos that survive in museum collections
duhos, that survive in museum collections,
duhos that survive in museum collections,
duhos, that survive in museum collections
items.explanation: “that survive in museum collections” is a restrictive clause: it identifies which duhos are meant (the surviving ones), so it takes no commas. The whole phrase “The duhos that survive in museum collections” is the subject of “display,” and no comma separates a subject from its verb.

B.why_wrong: A clause beginning with “that” is restrictive and can't be set off with commas as if it were extra information.

C.why_wrong: The comma after “collections” separates the subject from its verb, “display.”

D.why_wrong: The comma before “that” cuts off a restrictive clause from the noun it identifies.

items.notes: Subject: history and art (Taíno ceremonial seats). Band 6: two slots around a restrictive that-clause in subject position (6181924a), every wrong option failing on a rule. No person named.

band7.why: Target 6. 6181924a (band 6) shape: two slots around a restrictive that-clause in subject position, every distractor a plain rule error (commas around a that-clause, comma between subject and verb); no band-7 move.

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between long independent clauses
items.passage: In 1951, Soviet chemist Boris Belousov prepared a chemical mixture that alternated back and forth between colorless and yellow at regular ______ the editors of the journal to which he submitted his findings rejected them, dismissing such a reaction as impossible.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: Both “In 1951, Soviet chemist Boris Belousov prepared a chemical mixture that alternated ... at regular intervals” and “the editors of the journal to which he submitted his findings rejected them” are independent clauses. A comma plus the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them, and “but” fits the contrast between the striking result and its rejection.

A.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two independent clauses run together.

B.why_wrong: A comma alone can't join two independent clauses.

C.why_wrong: No comma belongs after “but” here; nothing interrupts the second clause.

items.notes: Subject: science (chemistry: the oscillating reaction Belousov observed in 1951; the duration of the oscillation is not stated, rejected as impossible). Plan cell says band 7, but S1_comma_conj has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/boundaries.md), so written as a strong band 6 and band_target set to 6, as WAVE.md directs. Hard from a 22-word clause 1 and a long subject in clause 2 (“the editors of the journal to which he submitted his findings”). No semicolon or period option.

fixes: “for nearly an hour” (an unchecked detail of a real chemist’s result) generalised to “back and forth ... at regular intervals” (passage now 41 words, was 39); blank and options moved from “hour” to “intervals”, explanation updated

band7.why: S1_comma_conj has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 on 59094d87: a 22-word clause 1, a long clause-2 subject (“the editors of the journal to which he submitted his findings”), and the “, but,” trap.

items.subtype: Semicolons between series items that contain commas, plus the comma before an item's appositive
items.passage: Swiss artist Sophie Taeuber-Arp undertook projects as diverse as Dada Head, a painted sculpture of turned ______ a 1918 puppet play for which she created the marionettes; and the Aubette, a Strasbourg entertainment complex whose interiors she helped redesign.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The three items in the series contain commas of their own, as the semicolon before “and the Aubette” shows, so a semicolon must separate “Dada Head, a painted sculpture of turned wood” from “King Stag.” A comma is then needed after “King Stag” before the phrase that describes it, “a 1918 puppet play ....”

A.why_wrong: A comma between the first two items doesn't match the semicolon used before the last item; items that contain commas are separated by semicolons.

C.why_wrong: The semicolon is right, but without a comma after “King Stag,” the descriptive phrase “a 1918 puppet play ...” runs into the title.

D.why_wrong: A colon can't separate two items in a series.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Sophie Taeuber-Arp: Dada Head, 1920; the marionettes for King Stag, 1918; the Aubette in Strasbourg, 1920s). Band 6: a8fa749a shape, two slots (series semicolon, comma before the item's appositive), the revealing semicolon (after “marionettes”) 10 words past the blank.

band7.why: Target 6. Close to a8fa749a (band 6): series semicolon plus the comma before the second item’s description, the revealing semicolon after “marionettes” 10 words past the blank. The band-7 series items (aaa1907f, db24ecc9) add a restrictive or supplement rule inside the first item; this one does not.

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing sentence appositive
items.passage: Turned away by many banks, Japanese immigrants in early-twentieth-century California often financed farms and businesses through tanomoshi, associations whose members contributed to a shared fund each month and took turns collecting the whole ______ arrangement that, with no written contract, depended entirely on trust among members.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Turned away by many banks, Japanese immigrants ... took turns collecting the whole sum” is a complete clause, and “an arrangement that ... depended entirely on trust among members” is a noun phrase that sums it up. A comma correctly attaches this trailing phrase to the clause.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “an arrangement that ... depended entirely on trust” has no main verb of its own (“depended” belongs to the that-clause).

C.why_wrong: “An arrangement that, with no written contract, depended entirely on trust among members” can't stand alone as a sentence; its only verb is inside the that-clause.

D.why_wrong: “and” would join the clause to a noun phrase that isn't a clause, so the sentence doesn't hold together.

items.notes: Subject: social science (economic history: tanomoshi rotating credit groups among Japanese immigrants in California). S2_trailing has only band-7 official items, so it is written as a plain hard band 6 on them: a sentence appositive whose relative clause holds the only finite verb (0b005ae2 shape, simplified), so B and C look like they start a clause.

band7.why: Target 6, but it reads band 7: a sentence appositive whose only finite verb sits inside its relative clause behind an interrupter (“an arrangement that, with no written contract, depended”), the 0b005ae2 and e67f9967 shape, with the 0b005ae2 menu (semicolon, period, and “, and” in place of the glued option) in a 46-word run after an introductory participle. All S2_trailing officials are band 7.

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: For decades, pilots’ reports of brief red flashes high above distant thunderstorms drew little scientific interest. In 1989, researchers testing a low-light camera in Minnesota recorded one on video by ______ the phenomenon, now known as a sprite, has since been caught on camera thousands of times.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 1989, researchers ... recorded one on video by accident” and “the phenomenon ... has since been caught on camera thousands of times” are both independent clauses. A comma plus the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone can't join two independent clauses.

B.why_wrong: No comma belongs after “and”; the second clause begins with its subject, “the phenomenon.”

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two independent clauses run together.

items.notes: Subject: science (atmospheric physics: red sprites, first recorded by chance in Minnesota in 1989). Medium: clause 2's subject carries an appositive pair (“now known as a sprite”). Researchers unnamed.

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: In 1206, engineer Ismail al-Jazari completed The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices, which describes some fifty machines in detailed drawings and text. Many of these devices, such as a mechanical band of musicians, were designed to ______ others, including several water-raising pumps, did useful work.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Many of these devices ... were designed to entertain” and “others, including several water-raising pumps, did useful work” are both independent clauses. A comma plus “but” correctly joins them and marks the contrast between amusement and practical use.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone can't join two independent clauses.

C.why_wrong: When “but” joins two independent clauses this long, a comma is needed before it.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two independent clauses run together.

items.notes: Subject: history (history of technology: al-Jazari's book of 1206, its automata and water-raising machines). Medium: both clauses carry an interrupting example set off by commas.

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a short participial phrase
items.passage: In the 1980s, archaeologists excavating ‘Ain Ghazal, a Neolithic settlement near Amman, Jordan, found two buried caches of human figures, some nearly a meter tall, sculpted from lime plaster over bundles of ______ about 9,000 years ago, the statues are among the oldest large-scale representations of the human form.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “sculpted from lime plaster over bundles of reeds.” “Made about 9,000 years ago” describes “the statues,” the subject of the next sentence (“the statues are among the oldest ...”), so a period is needed after “reeds.”

A.why_wrong: The comma attaches “made about 9,000 years ago” to the first sentence, leaving “the statues are among the oldest ...” joined to it by a comma alone.

B.why_wrong: Without punctuation, “reeds made about 9,000 years ago” runs the two sentences together, and “the statues are ...” is then spliced on with a comma.

C.why_wrong: “and” can't join these two long independent clauses without a comma, and “and made about 9,000 years ago, the statues are” doesn't form a grammatical sentence.

items.notes: Subject: history (archaeology: the lime plaster statues of ‘Ain Ghazal, Jordan). Medium: a 5-word participial opener before clause 2's subject. No semicolon option. Archaeologists unnamed.

items.subtype: Closing comma of a pair around an appositive, inside a closing quotation mark
items.passage: Tejano singer Lydia Mendoza began recording in the late 1920s and performed for nearly six decades. Her breakthrough, a 1934 recording of the song “Mal ______ established her as one of the earliest celebrities of Spanish-language music in the United States.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The comma after “breakthrough” opens the appositive “a 1934 recording of the song ‘Mal Hombre,’” which renames “Her breakthrough,” so a matching comma must close it before the verb “established.” In American style, the comma goes inside the closing quotation mark.

B.why_wrong: Without a closing comma, the appositive opened after “breakthrough” is never closed.

C.why_wrong: A dash can't close an appositive that was opened with a comma.

D.why_wrong: A semicolon can't separate the subject “Her breakthrough” from its verb, “established.”

items.notes: Subject: arts (music: Lydia Mendoza, “Mal Hombre,” 1934). Medium: the partner comma sits 7 words before the blank; the blank falls at a closing quotation mark (rw_options now handles quote marks).

fixes: explanation: nested double quotes around “Mal Hombre” changed to single quotes

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory participial phrase
items.passage: Encouraged by Russian ballerina Anna Pavlova to investigate the classical dance traditions of her own ______ Rukmini Devi Arundale studied a South Indian form now known as Bharatanatyam and in 1936 established Kalakshetra, an influential academy in Chennai.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Encouraged by Russian ballerina Anna Pavlova to investigate the classical dance traditions of her own country” is an introductory phrase describing Rukmini Devi Arundale, the subject of the main clause. A comma correctly separates the introductory phrase from that clause.

A.why_wrong: “and” would join the introductory phrase to a clause as if both were clauses; the phrase has no subject or main verb of its own.

B.why_wrong: A comma is needed to separate a long introductory phrase from the subject of the main clause.

D.why_wrong: “Encouraged by Russian ballerina Anna Pavlova to investigate the classical dance traditions of her own country” can't stand alone as a sentence.

items.notes: Subject: arts (dance: Rukmini Devi Arundale, Pavlova's encouragement, Kalakshetra founded in 1936). Medium: a 16-word introductory past-participial phrase.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a long subject and its verb
items.passage: The Inca Empire, which stretched roughly 4,000 kilometers along the Andes, had neither horses nor wheeled vehicles. Still, official messages passed between relay runners called chasquis at stations a short distance apart along the imperial road ______ could travel some 240 kilometers in a single day.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the long phrase “official messages passed between relay runners ... along the imperial road network,” and its verb is “could travel.” No punctuation belongs between a subject and its verb.

A.why_wrong: A comma can't separate the subject from its verb, “could travel.”

B.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, but the words before the blank are only the subject.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon can't separate a subject from its verb; neither side is an independent clause.

items.notes: Subject: history (Inca relay runners, the chasquis). Medium: a 19-word subject with two participial modifiers before the verb (2.11 shape). No person named; khipu not mentioned (an existing item uses it).

items.subtype: Semicolons between series items that contain commas
items.passage: Ushahidi, a crisis-mapping platform that Kenyan bloggers and programmers created in 2008, has been used to chart violence after Kenya’s disputed 2007 election; requests for help after the 2010 earthquake in Haiti, many of them sent by text ______ and reports of problems at polling places in several countries.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The series lists three things the platform has charted, and the second item contains a comma (“requests for help after the 2010 earthquake in Haiti, many of them sent by text message”). A semicolon already separates the first two items, so a semicolon must also separate the second from the third.

A.why_wrong: A comma here doesn't match the semicolon after “election”; when items contain commas, semicolons separate them.

C.why_wrong: A colon can't separate items in a series.

D.why_wrong: Some punctuation is needed between the second and third items in the series.

items.notes: Subject: social science (technology and civic life: Ushahidi, created in Kenya in 2008, later used in Haiti in 2010). Medium: the matching semicolon is 15 words before the blank (2.16 shape). No person named.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: In a two-week experiment in a British supermarket, researchers alternated between playing French accordion music and German beer-hall music near a display ______ French and German wines. French wines outsold German ones when French music was playing, and vice versa.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “French and German wines” is the object of the preposition “of,” and no punctuation belongs between a preposition and its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon can't come between a preposition and its object.

B.why_wrong: A dash can't separate a preposition from its object.

D.why_wrong: A comma can't separate a preposition from its object.

items.notes: Subject: social science (consumer psychology: in-store music and wine choice, a British supermarket study of the late 1990s). Researchers unnamed.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a verb and its object
items.passage: In most of the world’s languages, a sentence’s subject comes before its object. Hixkaryana, a Cariban language spoken along the Nhamundá River in northern Brazil, typically ______ the object first, followed by the verb and then the subject.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “the object” is the direct object of the verb “puts,” and no punctuation belongs between a verb and its object.

B.why_wrong: A colon can't come between a verb and its object.

C.why_wrong: A comma can't separate a verb from its object.

D.why_wrong: A dash can't separate a verb from its object.

items.notes: Subject: language (Hixkaryana's object-verb-subject word order). No linguist named.

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: The hinged lip of the hammer orchid, native to Western Australia, looks and smells like a female thynnid ______ males attempting to carry it away are swung against the flower’s reproductive structures.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The hinged lip of the hammer orchid ... looks and smells like a female thynnid wasp” and “males attempting to carry it away are swung against the flower’s reproductive structures” are both independent clauses. A comma plus “and” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two independent clauses run together.

B.why_wrong: A comma is needed before “and” when it joins two independent clauses like these.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone can't join two independent clauses.

items.notes: Subject: science (botany: hammer orchids of Western Australia and the thynnid wasps they deceive).

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory subordinate phrase
items.passage: Ethiopian philosopher Zera Yacob completed his Hatata, or “Inquiry,” in 1667. While hiding in a cave to escape religious ______ he had begun to question the doctrines of every faith he knew, resolving to accept only what reason could confirm.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “While hiding in a cave to escape religious persecution” is an introductory element, and the main clause begins with its subject, “he.” A comma correctly separates the introductory element from the main clause.

A.why_wrong: “and” would join the introductory phrase to the main clause as if both were clauses, which leaves the sentence ungrammatical.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon can't follow “While hiding in a cave to escape religious persecution,” which isn't an independent clause.

D.why_wrong: “While hiding in a cave to escape religious persecution” can't stand alone as a sentence.

items.notes: Subject: philosophy (Zera Yacob, the Hatata of 1667, his years hiding in a cave).

items.subtype: Direct question after a question word: inverted order and question mark
items.passage: In East Africa, the assassin bug Acanthaspis petax piles the bodies of ants it has eaten onto its back, binding them together with a sticky secretion. Why ______ Experiments suggest that this camouflage protects the insect from jumping spiders.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: does the bug carry this load.
does the bug carry this load?
items.explanation: “Why” begins a direct question, so the helping verb comes before the subject (“does the bug carry”) and the sentence ends with a question mark. The next sentence then answers the question.

A.why_wrong: A direct question beginning with “Why” needs inverted word order (“does the bug carry”), not statement order.

B.why_wrong: The word order is right for a direct question, but a direct question must end with a question mark.

D.why_wrong: Statement order with a period leaves “Why the bug carries this load” as a fragment rather than a question.

items.notes: Subject: science (entomology: the ant-corpse disguise of an East African assassin bug). Direct form with “Why” (b1 used an embedded “how,” b2 a direct “What”). Researchers unnamed.

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
items.passage: Since the late 1950s, American textile artist Sheila Hicks has made hundreds of what she calls minimes, small woven studies created on a portable wooden ______ them to experiment with colors, materials, and techniques that she may later use in her large-scale installations.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Since the late 1950s, American textile artist Sheila Hicks has made hundreds of ... minimes, small woven studies created on a portable wooden loom” is a complete clause. “using them to experiment with colors, materials, and techniques ...” is a participial phrase that adds information about Hicks, so a comma correctly attaches it to the clause.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon can't join a clause to the phrase “using them to experiment with colors ...,” which has no subject or main verb.

C.why_wrong: “Using them to experiment with colors, materials, and techniques ...” can't stand alone as a sentence.

D.why_wrong: “and” would join the clause to a phrase that isn't parallel with it, so the sentence doesn't hold together.

items.notes: Subject: arts (textiles: Sheila Hicks's minimes, woven on a small portable loom since the 1950s). Trailing -ing phrase rather than the which-clause of most earlier S2_trailing easy items.

items.subtype: Opening comma of a pair around a nonrestrictive which-clause
items.passage: Japanese novelist Yasunari Kawabata is celebrated for works such as Snow Country, but throughout a career spanning five decades he also composed more than 140 extremely brief stories. These ______ he called “palm-of-the-hand stories,” frequently occupy no more than two pages.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “which he called ‘palm-of-the-hand stories’” adds information about “These miniatures” and is closed by the comma after “stories.” A matching comma is needed before “which” to open the element, so that the subject “These miniatures” connects to the verb “occupy.”

A.why_wrong: Without a comma before “which,” the comma after “stories” has no partner and separates the subject from its verb.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon can't follow “These miniatures,” which isn't an independent clause.

C.why_wrong: “These miniatures.” isn't a sentence, and “Which he called ... frequently occupy no more than two pages” isn't a grammatical sentence either.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Kawabata's palm-of-the-hand stories). 1.10 shape: the blank opens the which-clause, its partner comma sits 4 words later inside the closing quotation mark.

fixes: explanation: nested double quotes around “palm-of-the-hand stories” changed to single quotes
